chunks: And regarding the knee, if it breaks and is set without a defect or flaw, its compensation is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars. So if it is fractured, its compensation is four-fifths of the wergild of its breaking, being one hundred and sixty Dinars; and the compensation for its exposure is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and the compensation for the displacement of its bones is one hundred and seventy-five Dinars, from which the compensation for its breaking is one hundred Dinars, and regarding the displacement of its bone is fifty Dinars, and regarding its exposure is twenty-five Dinars; and regarding bruising in it which does not heal, is thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar; and regarding its piercing is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and the compensation for its bruising is one-quarter of the wergild of its breaking, being fifty Dinars. So if it is bruised and becomes defective, regarding it is one-third of the wergild of the soul, being three hundred and thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar. So if it was disjointed, regarding it is three parts from the break, being thirty Dinars.
ai.seo_question: What is the compensation for a broken knee in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This passage from al-Kafi outlines the precise monetary compensation (diyah) for various knee injuries, reflecting the systematic application of *ta'zir* and *diyah* principles in Shia jurisprudence. It distinguishes between simple fractures, displacement, and bruising, providing a detailed legal framework for calculating damages based on the specific nature of the trauma. This granularity highlights the scholarly emphasis on justice and equitable restitution in personal injury cases.
